cells.tense: The hand that ends things is the same hand that will build the next thing, and right now you are holding the pen.
cells.ask: Pick the one ending you have been circling and finish it out loud today. Say the sentence that closes it — to the person, or alone — before you start on what comes after.
cells.core:
You are the one who ends things, and you do it without apology. Not loud, not dramatic — you clear the ground and then you build on it, and the building is slow and it does not stop.

That combination is rarer than it sounds. Plenty of people can end things and then sit in what's left, and plenty can build on ground that was not cleared first. You do the ending as a step toward the next thing, which is why you come across as steady. Notice something close at hand: when you go quiet for a day or two, you come back with the next move already clear. That is not a side habit. It is how the ending and the building stay in the same pair of hands. Keeping this costs something — it asks that you mean the ending you chose, not just the one that came easy.
cells.sheetLine: You clear the ground before you build, and you know that.
cells.verb: forcing a needed ending into reality through steady building
cells.place: the threshold where what was has to end for what comes next to begin

cells.tense: You are already living in the cleared room, bracing for an ending that has not arrived yet.
cells.ask: Name one thing you have been planning to end but have not decided to end. Say it out loud to someone who knows you — not to convince them, just to hear which way the wish actually points.
cells.core:
You are running the ending ahead of the ending. Somewhere ahead there is a version of your life where the thing is already gone and the new thing is already standing, and you are defending that version before the ground has moved.

The clearing is the skill. Rehearsing it is what costs you. Every quiet minute goes into measuring a structure that has not fallen, deciding in advance what you will feel when it goes, and the calm people count on is running on a what-if instead of on what is actually in the room. The people close to you can feel the rehearsal even when they cannot name it. The clearing works when it comes from something you actually see — a structure that needs to fall. Not one you decided in advance to knock down.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door you already walked through, watching it close.
cells.ask: Decide one thing this week that does not need anyone's approval — what stays, what goes, when it stops. Make the call, tell the one person it affects, and move on it the same day.
cells.core:
The ending happened. You are the one who did not move past it. The ground got cleared and you stayed in the doorway, looking at where the furniture used to be, and you have been calling that caution.

The clearing force is still in you. It just has nothing to build in, because the space you opened is being guarded instead of used. People around you notice the gap — they ask what you are going to do next, you say you are figuring it out, and you have been saying that for a while. What is missing is not the feeling. It is the decision. Someone has to say the thing is finished and mean it, and the someone is you. What you build next gets its shape from that call, not from the waiting.
cells.sheetLine: You have already cleared the room. You are still guarding the door.

cells.tense: The clearing is already going on around you, and you have been describing it as something that is happening to you.
cells.ask: Say out loud that one thing in your life is ending because you chose it — no hedging, no 'it was time.' Then pick the first concrete thing you are building where it stood, and start it this week.
cells.core:
Things have been ending around you, and you describe each one as something the season did. A role changed, a routine stopped, someone left — and the telling has no one in it.

The clearing was yours. You are the one who let it end, or ended it, or stopped holding on to something that was already going. That part of you is not in your own account of yourself, which means the next thing you build arrives with no one standing under it. The people who watch you see someone who makes room and then wonders why the room is empty. The nerve to say 'this is mine' about the endings is the same nerve the building needs. It does not come out of nowhere. It is one fire, and it wants tending and a name.
cells.sheetLine: The endings were your doing. You keep calling them the season.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is forcing structural change in their own life — for Too Much and Too Little especially, the record reports a capacity operating in one domain, not proof of what they're doing. A reader could reasonably say 'this is about a work project, not my whole life,' and the ask must still be useful if my read is wrong: it should be about one unavoidable thing of theirs, not a verdict on how they live. The sentence that serves the writer more than them is any line that tells them what they're 'really' feeling underneath the ending — the record does not license it, and I've cut it.
